synopsis: Robust-WAM adds future semantic supervision to an existing video-based robot policy while retaining its VAE video-prediction path. Learnable queries enter the action transformer, share positional codes with corresponding action steps, and learn to match frozen DINOv3 features of demonstrated future observations. The teacher and projection head disappear at inference, but the queries remain. Reported gains include FastWAM improving from 49.7% to 58.9% on LIBERO-Plus and GE-Act improving from 57.3% to 80.0% under real-robot illumination shifts. These results support the usefulness of the added supervision; they do not independently establish the authors’ explanation that appearance-invariant semantics preserve pretrained dynamics knowledge. [E02, E05, E06, E09, E14]

problem.text: The authors identify a representation tradeoff: video-generation pretraining supplies useful dynamics knowledge in reconstruction-oriented VAE latents, but those latents also encode appearance variations that can disrupt control. Rebuilding prediction in semantic latents changes the representation space and loses direct reuse of that video pretraining. Robust-WAM asks whether future semantic supervision can improve an existing WAM’s action representation while retaining its generative formulation.

contributions.text: A post-training modification that places future semantic supervision inside a pretrained video WAM’s action stream without replacing its VAE tokenization or video objective.
A query-to-action temporal correspondence rule, with one query per future frame and camera view, using the host policy’s existing positional encoding.
The reported experiments show aggregate OOD success improvements for two action-expert WAMs and one unified WAM, with clean performance maintained or slightly increased.

inputs: Current observation o_t and language instruction ℓ, conditioning the host WAM. [E04]
During training: demonstrated action chunks and corresponding future frames from each camera. [E04, E06]
Noised action tokens, host video hidden states, and learnable semantic queries; ground-truth teacher embeddings are supervision, never query inputs. [E04, E06]
outputs: An action chunk through the host policy’s original action head. [E04, E06]
Future VAE-latent predictions through the retained video-training path. [E04]
Auxiliary predictions of future DINOv3 features during training; internal query states remain available to action attention at inference. [E06]

steps.name: Retain the host world-action computation
steps.detail: The video stream denoises future-frame VAE latents. Action blocks attend to video hidden states while predicting action velocities. This connection supplies generative features to action prediction; Robust-WAM preserves the host architecture and objectives.

steps.name: Insert temporally matched queries
steps.detail: Prepend K = T_f C learnable tokens to the L action tokens. Query j for any camera receives the positional code of action token min(jΔ, L). Original action indices remain unchanged. If the video horizon exceeds the action horizon, trailing queries share the final action position.

steps.name: Supervise future semantics
steps.detail: A frozen DINOv3 encoder produces a CLS target for each demonstrated future frame and camera. After action-block processing, a learned linear head maps query outputs into the teacher space. Cosine alignment supplements the existing video and action losses; the original action head still receives only its usual action-token outputs.

steps.name: Preserve architecture-specific attention
steps.detail: For action-expert hosts, queries join expert self-attention and attend to the video tower. In LingBot-VA, they enter the unified action segment with matching sequence, frame and noise IDs, allowing same-step interaction while preserving the host’s autoregressive ordering.

training.text: The implementation uses eight future frames and frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 CLS targets of dimension 768, extracted offline. Two-camera LIBERO and real-robot setups use 16 queries; three-camera RoboTwin uses 24. The alignment weight is 0.1.

Each baseline–Robust-WAM pair shares data, schedule and optimization settings. Action horizon and frame stride follow the host’s released recipe. The VAE encoder and semantic teacher are explicitly frozen; preserving the video branch does not establish that all its weights are frozen.

inference.text: Remove DINOv3 and the alignment head, retain the learned queries, and use the host action sampler. Section 3.1 describes integrating action velocity from Gaussian noise at s = 1 to a clean chunk at s = 0. No future ground-truth observation is required.

The semantic addition influences actions through transformer features, not a separate inverse-dynamics decoder or optimization against teacher embeddings. Exact per-backbone inference schedules and how much of each chunk is executed before feedback are not specified in this text.

equations.expression: x_s = sε + (1−s)x; a_s = sε′ + (1−s)a; L_WAM = E[||v^v_θ(x_s,s|o_t,ℓ)−(ε−x)||²] + λ_a E[||v^a_θ(a_s,s|H^v,o_t,ℓ)−(ε′−a)||²].
equations.explanation: Equations (1)–(3) train video and action velocity predictors with uniform flow time and independent Gaussian noise. x contains future VAE latents, a the demonstrated actions, and H^v the video features read by the action stream. Sampling integrates backward in s; λ_a comes from the host recipe.

equations.expression: K = T_f C; k = (j−1)C+c; τ_j = min(jΔ,L); h = [q; h^a].
equations.explanation: Equations (4)–(5) associate future frame j and camera c with query k. Since frame o_(t+jΔ) follows action a_(t+jΔ−1), its query reuses action position jΔ, clamped to the available action horizon. Here L = H is the number of action tokens.

equations.expression: L_align = (1/K) Σ_k [1−cos(g(h̄_k),z*_k)]; L = L_WAM + λ_align L_align.
equations.explanation: Equations (6)–(7) align transformed query outputs h̄_k, projected by linear head g, with frozen future-frame teacher targets z*_k. This is auxiliary supervision, not an additional inference-time loss.

results.setting: FastWAM trained on the four standard LIBERO suites; evaluated on clean LIBERO and all LIBERO-Plus perturbed tasks.
results.comparison: Baseline: 49.7 OOD; 97.6 clean. Reported gains: 9.2 and 0.3 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Reported simulated execution success improves substantially in aggregate under perturbations, with no observed clean-performance loss.

results.setting: GE-Act under the corresponding standard-LIBERO training and LIBERO-Plus evaluation protocol.
results.comparison: Baseline: 78.0 OOD; 96.5 clean. Reported gains: 2.9 and 0.8 percentage points.
results.interpretation: This is the highest aggregate LIBERO-Plus success reported in Table 1. Matched within-backbone comparisons are more informative about the modification than cross-family rankings.

results.setting: LingBot-VA and its variant trained on the same 2,500 clean demonstrations for 15K steps; evaluated with 100 episodes per task on clean and randomized splits.
results.comparison: Baseline: 29.8 randomized; 81.2 clean. Randomized gain: 4.6 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Reported simulated execution results support transfer to a unified architecture, although randomized success remains well below clean success.

results.setting: FastWAM on the full LIBERO-Plus suite; shared data and schedule, with 16 queries for these variants.
results.comparison: Without temporal PE: 55.0; current-frame targets: 52.7; baseline: 49.7.
results.interpretation: The reported differences support both temporal indexing and future targets in this setting. They do not directly measure semantic prediction accuracy.

results.setting: FastWAM on LIBERO-Plus with a shared training schedule.
results.comparison: DINOv3 Patch: 57.0; DA3: 56.8; DINOv3 CLS + DA3: 56.5.
results.interpretation: CLS performs best among tested choices. This is not a pure feature-content comparison: patch alignment changes the head, and combining targets doubles the query count from 16 to 32.

results.task: Physical tabletop manipulation under illumination shifts
results.setting: Franka Research 3; Carrot→Bread, Kiwi→Basket and Stack Cups. Standard-light training; 25 standard, 25 purple and 25 cyan evaluation rollouts per task and policy.
results.metric: Average executed-task success (%) and InD-to-OOD gap (percentage points)
results.value: Robust-WAM on GE-Act: 80.0 OOD; 82.7 InD; gap 2.7.
results.interpretation: These are reported physical robot successes, not video metrics. Keeping objects, cameras and scene fixed isolates illumination changes, but limits the demonstrated real-world generalization scope.

limitations.text: Aggregate improvements are not universal across perturbations: FastWAM’s robot-initial-state success falls from 44.4% to 43.4%, and GE-Act’s lighting success falls from 95.4% to 95.2%.

The comparison with LDA-1B does not isolate the value of retaining generative pretraining. Architectures and training recipes differ, so the authors’ enhance-versus-replace conclusion exceeds what that comparison alone establishes.

The reported success tables provide no seed variability or confidence intervals. The physical study covers three tasks and two unseen lighting conditions, leaving broader deployment robustness untested.

Improved control does not directly demonstrate appearance invariance, accurate semantic foresight, or preservation of pretrained dynamics knowledge. The reported experiments do not separately quantify these mechanisms.

Dropping the teacher and head avoids their inference computation, but retained queries still enlarge attention sequences. The supplied experiments do not quantify latency, memory overhead or training compute.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the host WAM checkpoints and recipes, synchronized action–future-frame demonstrations, the frozen VAE encoder, and DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Implement the query positional mapping, preserve the host attention rules, cache teacher CLS targets, and add the weighted cosine objective.

The text delegates action horizons, frame strides and optimization details to host releases. It does not enumerate exact checkpoint revisions, teacher-image preprocessing, per-backbone denoising settings, or physical demonstration counts. A project-page link does not establish code availability; no code was inspected or experiment reproduced for this report.

A focused reproduction would compare FastWAM baseline, full future alignment, no-temporal-PE alignment and current-frame alignment on LIBERO-Plus under matched data and compute. Multiple seeds, per-axis success and measured inference overhead would test the central mechanism more directly than another cross-model ranking.

reasoning.text: The snapshot is defensible at the level of the added method: Robust-WAM contributes auxiliary future-feature alignment and supports multiple host architectures, making 'Other mechanisms' and 'Outside quadrants' appropriate for that addition. Section 3.3 explicitly distinguishes separate action experts from a unified transformer; joint training alone is not the architecture evidence. The underlying hosts still perform video–action modeling, so 'Not applicable' should not imply that those implementations lack an architecture. 'Latent prediction & JEPA' fits the broad future-representation theme, but the proposed component is DINOv3-supervised query alignment, not a replacement JEPA generative path. No taxonomy values are revised.

discussionQuestions: Would the advantage of future targets persist against equally costly query regularizers or alternative teachers under repeated-seed evaluation? [E12]
How does sharing the final action position affect foresight when the video horizon extends beyond the action chunk? [E05]
Can direct feature-invariance and video-dynamics measurements substantiate the explanation for the control gains? [E02, E09, E14]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, project-page line and arXiv version stamp
evidence.detail: The title and author list match the catalog; the supplied artifact identifies arXiv:2608.05903v2, dated 7 August 2026, and provides a project-page URL.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Abstract and Section 1 Introduction
evidence.detail: The authors motivate semantic alignment through appearance sensitivity in reconstruction latents and the cost of abandoning VAE-space video pretraining.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2 Related Work, Representation Alignment in Robot Learning
evidence.detail: The paper distinguishes its WAM integration and explicit query–action temporal correspondence from earlier future-representation alignment in standalone policies.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.1, Equations (1)–(3) and inference paragraph
evidence.detail: The formulation uses a frozen VAE encoder, coupled video/action flow losses, video hidden states attended by action blocks, and action sampling by integration from noise to data.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Per-Frame Semantic Query Tokens, Equations (4)–(5)
evidence.detail: Queries are indexed by future frame and camera, prepended to actions, and assigned matching action positional encodings with a clamp at the final action position.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Semantic Foresight Targets and Alignment Objective, Equations (6)–(7)
evidence.detail: Frozen future-frame DINOv3 CLS embeddings supervise projected query outputs through cosine loss. Teacher features are never query inputs; the teacher and linear head are removed at inference while queries remain.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.3, Action-Expert WAMs and Unified WAMs
evidence.detail: Action-expert implementations insert queries into the expert sequence. Unified LingBot-VA assigns corresponding action sequence, frame and noise IDs under the original flex-attention mask.

The implementation specifies eight future frames, DINOv3 ViT-B/16 CLS dimension 768, offline targets, alignment weight 0.1, and 16 or 24 queries depending on camera count. Host recipes determine horizons and training settings.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2 Setup; PDF p. 7, Table 1, FastWAM and GE-Act baseline/Robust-WAM rows
evidence.detail: Clean/OOD success is 97.6/49.7 for FastWAM and 97.9/58.9 with alignment; corresponding GE-Act values are 96.5/78.0 and 97.3/80.9. Table 1 reports averages over evaluation trials without uncertainty columns.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2, Init and Light rows and per-axis results discussion
evidence.detail: FastWAM initial-state success changes from 44.4 to 43.4, while GE-Act lighting success changes from 95.4 to 95.2. The table separately reports seven perturbation axes.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.3 Setup; PDF p. 8, Table 3 and Results
evidence.detail: LingBot-VA variants use 2,500 clean demonstrations, 15K training steps and 100 evaluation episodes per task. The results paragraph confirms randomized success of 29.8 versus 34.4 and unchanged clean success of 81.2.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.4 Setup and Table 4, alignment-target and query-design rows
evidence.detail: CLS, patch, DA3 and combined targets score 58.9, 57.0, 56.8 and 56.5. Removing temporal PE yields 55.0; current-frame supervision yields 52.7. Patch alignment uses an MLP; the combined variant uses 32 rather than 16 queries.

The physical study uses a Franka Research 3 and three tabletop tasks. Training uses standard lighting; evaluation changes illumination to purple and cyan while keeping the scene, objects and cameras fixed. Each task/policy receives 25 rollouts per condition.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 5, Avg. columns, and Section 4.5 Results
evidence.detail: GE-Act averages 80.0 InD and 57.3 OOD success with a 22.7-point gap. Robust-WAM averages 82.7 and 80.0 with a 2.7-point gap; these aggregate values are also stated in the results paragraph.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.2 Results, LDA-1B comparison; PDF p. 8, Section 4.3 Results, LDA-1B comparison
evidence.detail: The authors use comparisons against semantic-latent LDA-1B to argue that semantic representations are more effective when enhancing retained video-generation priors than replacing them.
